A rare genetic mutation called pseudo-melanism has resulted in roughly half of the tigers in India's Similipal Tiger Reserve sporting coats with far more black than those of usual tigers. This widespread coloration is a symptom of a shallow gene pool in a region that previously faced a dwindling tiger population, and could prove catastrophic if conservation officers aren't able to find these tigers more genetically diverse mates. The tiger (Panthera tigris) is the largest living cat species, recognised by its powerful body, sharp claws, muscular limbs, and distinctive orange coat covered in black stripes. Tigers are skilled hunters with exceptional night vision, strong jaws, and the ability to move quietly through dense vegetation. Unlike most cats, they are also excellent swimmers and often use rivers and lakes to cool down or travel. Tigers symbolise strength, courage, independence, and raw power. They inhabit forests, grasslands, mangroves, and other environments across parts of Asia. Unlike lions, tigers are generally solitary animals, patrolling large territories and hunting prey such as deer and wild boar. Despite their strength, they face serious threats from habitat loss, poaching, and conflicts with humans. Fun fact: Every tiger has a unique pattern of stripes, and the markings extend onto its skin beneath the fur. No two tigers have exactly the same stripe pattern.  #Tiger #PantheraTigris #Wildlife #BigCats #Nature

GUATEMALA’S LAST CIRCUS TIGERS. Seven tigers (Simba, Kimba, Jix, Chiquita, Nala, Africa and Kenia) have been removed from a circus and are now in the ADI Temporary Rescue Unit in Guatemala. They will be relocated to the ADI Wildlife Sanctuary in South Africa where they will live in huge natural, secure, enclosures with pools and space to roam for the rest of their lives. The tigers were removed by the Guatemalan animal welfare division, Unidad de Bienestar Animal (UBA), the Consejo Nacional de Areas Protegidas (CONAP) (wildlife), and police, with logistical support provided by Animal Defenders International (ADI) – trucks, crane, transport cages, and placed in an ADI Temporary Rescue Unit in Guatemala while they are prepared for their new lives. Following Guatemala’s law banning animal circuses, in 2018, Circo Rey Gitano refused to surrender their animals, leading to an 8-year legal battle with the government’s UBA to enforce the animal welfare law. The tigers have remained in their circus cages on trucks in the circus compound for almost a decade, with no effort to provide them with appropriate facilities – stored like equipment, no exercise enclosures, to be posed with for social media ‘likes’. Not images of ‘love’ but of possession and control. The circus lost all legal options and agreed to the removal of the tigers. They announced on social media they would give up the tigers, then deliberately put the tigers at risk during the seizure. They ensured the animals could not be removed without being sedated, piling old cars, heaps of metal and other junk around them. Despite the removal date being weeks after a court order directing them to hand the animals to the government. The owner knew that by blocking access the animals would need to be sedated to be removed. Even worse, they fed the tigers knowing this would complicate sedation and put them at risk. All caring owners know animals must not be fed prior to sedation. These were not the actions of people putting the welfare of animals first. UBA’s team of eight veterinarians who entered the circus to remove the tigers and were constantly disrupted during the procedures. Even in the street, when the animals were being loaded into the ADI cages and the sedation was being reversed, circus people were shouting, jostling and trying to pull the covers off the cages. Inside the circus, one tiger suffered complications but the veterinary team addressed the problem, and no animals died. The Gitano circus workers were present and aware of this, but have continued to lie to the Gautemalan public, claiming one died. All the tigers were fully conscious when they were unloaded at the ADI TRU that night, and were filmed safe and alive by Guatemalan television the following day. The TRU is run by ADI, under the authority of the Government of Guatemala, overseen by Unidad de Bienestar Animal (UBA) and Consejo Nacional de Areas Protegidas (CONAP) departments. ADI is covering running costs, food, care, veterinary treatment and additional armed security due to the threatening situation caused by the circus. The animals are in quarantine and are being prepared for the move to the ADI Wildlife Sanctuary, in compliance with international veterinary requirements for blood tests for disease, vaccinations, treatment for parasites. At Circo Rey Gitano the tigers were kept in tiny cages on the backs of trucks, no space to run, no grass, no pools.  At the ADIWS each tiger will have at least 10,000 square meters / 107,639 square feet of natural open space, pools and houses. They will be able to run at full speed, sun overhead, grass under their feet. ADI thanks the Government of Guatemala’s UBA and CONAP for enforcing the law and taking action to give these animals a better life and also, thanks the majority of the public in Guatemala.
